opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think one of the big problems with deep learning today is that architecture design is basically alchemy. People try things, they tweak things, they add a skip connection here, a normalization layer there, and if the numbers on the benchmark go up, it gets published. There's very little understanding of *why* a given architecture works, and so there's very little guidance on how to find the next one.

What TensorLogic does is give you a single language in which all of these architectures can be written down very compactly, and, crucially, in the same terms as logic. The basic construct in TensorLogic is the tensor equation. And the key observation is that a logical rule and an Einstein summation are really the same thing. A Datalog rule is a join followed by a projection, and that's exactly what a tensor contraction does, just over Boolean values instead of reals. So once you see that, a convolutional network, a transformer, a graph neural network, a kernel machine, a probabilistic graphical model, they're all just a handful of tensor equations. A transformer is maybe a dozen lines.

Now, why does that help you choose and refine architectures? A few reasons.

First, when everything is expressed in one language, you can actually compare architectures. You can see that this one is that one with an extra index, or with a different nonlinearity, or with one join replaced by another. The design space becomes something you can see and reason about, instead of a zoo of papers and PyTorch code where the essential structure is buried under implementation details.

Second, because the equations have a logical reading, you can bring in knowledge. If you know something about your domain, you can write it down as rules, and those rules are the same kind of object as the neural layers. So instead of hoping the network rediscovers that structure from data, you put it in, and then learning refines it. That's a much more principled way to design an architecture: it's derived from what you know about the problem rather than from trial and error.

Third, and this is the part I'm most excited about, it makes architecture search itself a learning problem in a natural space. If architectures are sets of tensor equations, then searching over architectures is like searching over programs or over rule sets, which is what inductive logic programming and structure learning have been doing for decades. You can grow and prune equations, you can learn the relations themselves via embeddings, and you can go back and forth between the soft, embedded version and the hard, logical version. There's a temperature parameter that lets you go from purely deductive reasoning, with no hallucinations, to analogical reasoning in embedding space. So you get to choose where on that spectrum your model should sit for a given problem, which is an architectural decision that today people make implicitly and blindly.

And then finally there's interpretability. When you look at a trained TensorLogic model, you can extract the rules it's effectively using. So refining an architecture isn't just "the loss went down"; you can actually inspect what the model learned, see where it's wrong, and fix that piece.

So in short, I think it turns architecture design from a craft into something closer to an engineering discipline, and ultimately into something that can be largely automated. That's what we need if we want AI to stop being a bag of tricks and become a real science.

r002.rationale: It describes encoding domain knowledge as rules that learning can refine, but does not state that these rules express beliefs about structure without fully determining the architecture.

r003.rationale: It mentions moving between soft embedded and hard logical reasoning, but does not characterize structural equations as soft priors rather than mandatory constraints.

r004.rationale: It describes growing and pruning equations to search architectures, and inspecting learned behavior to identify errors and fix the corresponding piece.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the first thing to understand is that right now architecture design is basically alchemy. You have this zoo of architectures, transformers, convolutional nets, graph neural networks, and so on, and each one is described in its own notation, with its own code, its own tricks. If you want to compare two of them, let alone combine the best parts of each, you're essentially doing trial and error. There's no common language in which you can look at them side by side and see what they actually have in common and where they differ.

What Tensor Logic does is give you that language. The core idea is very simple: a logical rule and an Einstein summation are the same thing. A rule like "A implies C if B" is a tensor contraction over the shared index. Once you see that, every neural architecture becomes a small set of tensor equations, and they're all written in the same notation. A transformer is a few lines. A convolutional net is a few lines. A kernel machine, a graphical model, a logic program, same thing. And when everything is in one language, the differences stop being hidden in thousands of lines of PyTorch and become visible as differences in the equations.

So for a researcher, the payoff is that you can reason about architectures instead of just running them. You can see that attention is really a kind of soft database join, or that a convolution is a rule with a particular index structure, and then you can ask, well, what if I change this index, or add this contraction, or make this part symbolic and that part learned? Those become principled questions rather than random perturbations. And because the whole thing is differentiable, you don't give up any of the learning machinery. You just gain the ability to see what you're doing.

The other piece I think is important is the knob between pure deductive reasoning and pure embedding-style reasoning. In Tensor Logic you can control how "soft" the inference is, essentially by a temperature. At zero temperature you get exact logical reasoning, no hallucinations, and as you turn it up you get the kind of analogical generalization that embeddings give you. That means an architecture isn't just a fixed thing anymore; you can refine it along that axis depending on what the problem needs. For a lot of applications, especially where you care about reliability, that's exactly the dial people have been missing.

So in short, I see it as doing for neural architectures what differential equations did for physics. Once you have the right formalism, you stop collecting recipes and you start having a science.

astra-6.text:
I think TensorLogic can help turn architecture design into a more systematic process. Today, we have a lot of architectural ideas that work empirically, but it can be difficult to articulate precisely what assumptions they encode. A logical representation gives you a way to make those assumptions explicit, while the tensor representation gives you a way to carry out the computation and learn from data.

So you can ask: What relationships does this task require? What information should interact, and what structure should be preserved? Those questions can guide the architecture. Then, when the model fails, you have something more interpretable to examine: perhaps a relationship is missing, or a constraint is too restrictive. You can revise that structure and test it.

It doesn’t eliminate experimentation. The promise is to give experimentation a language in which you can reason about what you’re changing and why.

r004.rationale: It suggests revising a structure when a model fails, but does not clearly identify adding or modifying TensorLogic equations as the means of refining the structure based on learning results.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make the assumptions behind an architecture explicit. Today, designing a neural network involves a lot of intuition and trial and error. With TensorLogic, you can express the structure you want in logical terms and see how that translates into tensor operations.

That gives you a way to ask: What relationships does this architecture represent? What constraints does it impose? And if those assumptions don’t fit the problem, what should we change? You can then refine the structure as well as learn the parameters.

It doesn’t magically tell you which architecture will work best. You still need experiments. But it can make architecture design more systematic: you’re testing explicit hypotheses about the problem, with a language that connects those hypotheses to the computation.

r003.rationale: The response mentions constraints but does not characterize structural equations as soft priors rather than mandatory constraints.
